title: Parameter sets and fault finding
goals: Commission a drive in the right order: motor data, identification run, control, I/O, ramps and limits, backup
Work out a motor's full-load current from its plate, to check the motor data
Read a drive's fault log and turn each common trip into its likely causes
Work safely on a drive: wait, measure the DC bus, and disconnect it before insulation testing
Save, compare and restore a parameter set so a replacement drive runs like the old one
summary:
A drive does only what its **parameters** say. Commission in order:

1. **Motor data** from the plate: voltage, current, frequency, speed, power, power factor (cos φ). The drive models the motor from these, so they must be right, and match how the motor is connected (star or delta).
2. **Identification run** (autotune): **static** (the motor does not turn) or **rotating** (better; uncouple the load if you can). It measures the motor for vector control.
3. **Control**: V/f or vector; the **start/stop source** and **speed reference** (terminals, keypad, fieldbus).
4. **I/O**: digital inputs, relay outputs, analogue scaling.
5. **Ramps**, **current limit**, min and max speed, **stop mode**, **fault reactions** (what it does if the fieldbus is lost).
6. **Back up** the parameters and write down what you changed.

Full-load current to check against the plate: $I = \frac{P}{\sqrt{3}\,V \cos\varphi\,\eta}$.

**Fault finding** starts with the **fault log**: which fault, when, and the conditions at the time (current, bus voltage, frequency, temperature).

- **Overcurrent**: acceleration too fast, a jammed load, wrong motor data, a short in the cable or motor
- **DC overvoltage**: deceleration too fast or an overhauling load; no brake resistor
- **Undervoltage**: a supply dip or a lost phase
- **Earth fault**: insulation breaking down in the motor or cable (or very long cables)
- **Drive overtemperature**: blocked fan or filter, dirty heatsink, hot cabinet
- **Motor overtemperature**: the thermistor (PTC): overload, low speed with a fan-cooled motor, blocked cooling
- **Communication loss**: a fieldbus timeout

**Safety**: after isolation the DC bus stays charged: wait the time on the label and **measure** it before touching. **Disconnect the drive** before insulation-testing the motor or its cable: the test voltage can destroy the output stage.

formulas.name: Three-phase motor current
formulas.says: The shaft power, plus the motor's losses, at the supply voltage and power factor, gives the current it draws.
formulas.example: 7.5 kW, 400 V, cos φ 0.84, 89% efficient: $\frac{7500}{1.732 \times 400 \times 0.84 \times 0.89} = 14.5$ A.

bench.task: On a drive you look after, make a parameter record. Read only, unless you are authorised to commission it.
check: Save a backup (keypad, memory card or PC tool) and label it with the date and machine
List the parameters that differ from the defaults (most drives can show 'changed parameters')
Check the motor data against the motor plate, star or delta included
Read the fault log and note the last five faults with their times

cards.q: A failed drive is replaced with a new one of the same model. What must happen before it runs the conveyor?
options: Load the old parameter set, then check it
Nothing: the same model runs the same
Run it on the factory defaults first
Swap the motor for a matching new one
cards.why: A new drive has factory defaults: wrong motor data, wrong ramps, wrong I/O. Load the saved parameters (or set them up again from the record), check them, and only then run it. Without a backup, every setting has to be found again.

cards.title: Commissioning in the right order
cards.body:
1. **Motor data** from the plate
2. **Identification run** (autotune)
3. **Control**: V/f or vector; where start/stop and the speed reference come from
4. **I/O**: inputs, outputs, analogue scaling
5. **Ramps, limits, stop mode, fault reactions**
6. **Test**, then **back up** and record

Later steps rely on earlier ones: the identification run uses the motor data, and vector control needs the identification run.
cards.more:
It is like setting up a new phone: who you are first, then the apps.

Most drives have a start-up assistant that walks through steps 1 to 4. Many also have **macros** (application presets: 'conveyor', 'pump', 'fieldbus control') that set the I/O in one go; pick one first, then adjust, rather than setting every input by hand.

Step 5 is where a drive is made to suit the machine: a ramp too short trips on overcurrent; a stop mode of 'coast' on a conveyor lets it run on; a fault reaction of 'keep last speed' on lost comms can be dangerous on some machines.

Step 6 is the one most often skipped, and the one that saves the day when the drive dies.

items: Enter the motor data from its plate
Set the control mode and command sources
Set the I/O, ramps and limits
Test, then back up the parameters
cards.why: Each step builds on the one before: the motor model before vector control, the controls before testing, and the backup last, of the settings that work.

cards.title: Motor data, and checking it
cards.body:
The plate gives **voltage**, **current**, **frequency**, **speed**, **power**, **power factor** (cos φ) and often efficiency. Enter them for the way the motor is **connected**: a 400/690 V motor is **delta** on a 400 V drive, and its current is the 400 V figure.

A check: the full-load current should be about

$$I = \frac{P}{\sqrt{3}\,V \cos\varphi\,\eta}$$

Wrong motor data gives poor speed holding, overcurrent trips, or a motor that overheats without the drive noticing.
cards.more:
The drive builds a model of the motor from these numbers; vector control is only as good as the model.

Numbers: a 7.5 kW, 400 V motor with cos φ 0.84 and 89% efficiency. $\sqrt{3} \times 400 = 693$; $\times 0.84 \times 0.89 = 518$; $7500 \div 518 = 14.5$ A. If the plate says 14.6 A at 400 V, it all hangs together.

Star or delta matters: the same motor might say 400 V Δ 14.6 A / 690 V Y 8.4 A. On a 400 V drive, wired delta, enter 400 V and 14.6 A. Entering 8.4 A would make the drive think the motor is overloaded at half power; entering 690 V would make it run at the wrong flux.

The motor's overload protection in the drive uses the rated current too: set it right and the drive protects the motor.

cards.q: A motor plate says {p} kW, 400 V, cos φ {pf}, efficiency {eff}%. Roughly what full-load current should it draw?
cards.why: Shaft power plus losses (÷ efficiency), divided by √3 × V × power factor. If the plate's current is far from this, recheck what you have read, and the star or delta.
cards.hint: kW × 1000 for watts; efficiency as a decimal.

cards.title: The identification run
cards.body:
Vector control needs to know the motor's insides: stator resistance, inductances, magnetising current. The **identification run** (autotune) measures them.

- **Static**: the drive injects test currents without turning the motor. Good enough for many jobs, and safe with the load coupled.
- **Rotating**: the motor spins (at up to full speed) to measure more. Better results; **uncouple** the load if possible, and make sure the machine is safe to turn.

Redo it after changing the motor, or a long change to the motor cable.
cards.more:
Like a mechanic measuring an engine before tuning it: the better the measurements, the better the tuning.

Vector control works out how much of the current makes flux and how much makes torque, and that depends on the motor's resistances and inductances. With a good identification run, a drive can hold speed under load and give full torque at low speed. With a bad one, it may hunt, trip, or give weak torque.

A rotating run turns the motor without warning on the machine's own guarding: treat it like any test run. Some drives also do a short check every start (DC magnetising), which is not the same thing.

cards.q: When should the identification run be repeated?
options: After the motor is changed for a different one
Every time the drive is switched on
After changing the acceleration ramp
Never: it is done once at the factory
cards.why: It measures this motor (and its cable). A different motor, even of the same power, has different values. Ramps do not affect it.

cards.title: Start with the fault log
cards.body:
Most drives keep a **fault log**: which fault, when, and often the **conditions** at that moment: output current, DC bus voltage, frequency, temperatures, the state of the run command.

Read it before resetting anything. It tells you:

- **what** tripped, and **when** in the machine's cycle (starting, running, stopping)
- whether it is **new**, or has happened before at the same point
- the **numbers** that confirm or rule out a cause

Then reset and run once while watching, if it is safe to.
cards.more:
A fault code alone is a symptom; the conditions are the evidence.

Overcurrent with the frequency at 3 Hz and rising: tripped while accelerating. Overcurrent at 50 Hz steady: a jam, or a fault in the cable. DC overvoltage with the frequency falling: decelerating.

Patterns matter too: the same trip every Monday morning (cold grease), every afternoon (a hot cabinet), or after rain (water in a junction box: an earth fault).

Write down the log before resetting or powering down: some drives lose it, and someone else may reset it 'to get it going'.

cards.q: A drive has tripped. What is the most useful first step?
options: Read the fault log and its conditions
Reset it and run it to see what happens
Restore the factory default settings
Replace the drive with a spare
cards.why: The log says what tripped and under what conditions, which points at the cause. Resetting first can lose that and repeat the fault; defaults throw away the setup; a new drive with the same fault will trip too.

cards.title: The common trips and their causes
cards.body:
- **Overcurrent**: acceleration too fast for the inertia; a jam; wrong motor data; a short in the motor or cable
- **DC overvoltage**: deceleration too fast, or an overhauling load; no brake resistor
- **Undervoltage**: a supply dip; a lost phase; a weak supply when big loads start
- **Earth fault**: insulation failing in the motor or cable; water in a box; sometimes very long cables
- **Drive overtemperature**: fan failed, filters blocked, dirty heatsink, hot cabinet
- **Motor overtemperature** (thermistor): overload; running slowly for long with a shaft-mounted fan
- **Communication loss**: the fieldbus or network dropped out
cards.more:
Ask what the drive was doing at the moment it tripped.

Speeding up: current (overcurrent). Slowing down: energy coming back (overvoltage). Steady running: the load (overcurrent), the supply (undervoltage), heat (overtemperature), insulation (earth fault).

Motor overtemperature at low speed is a classic: a standard motor cools itself with a fan on its own shaft, so at 10 Hz it gets a fifth of the airflow. Long low-speed running needs derating or a separately powered fan.

An earth fault that comes and goes, especially in wet weather, is almost always insulation: test the motor and cable (with the drive disconnected).

cards.q: Match each trip with its most likely cause.
pairs: Water in the motor or a junction box
Shaft fan cooling too little at low speed
Blocked cabinet filters or a failed fan
cards.why: When it trips (speeding up, slowing down, running) and the conditions (weather, season, speed) narrow the cause down.

cards.title: Working safely on drives
cards.body:
- **Isolate and lock off** the drive's supply. The **DC bus capacitors stay charged**: wait at least the time on the label (often 5 to 15 minutes), then **measure** the DC bus (DC+ to DC−) before touching anything inside.
- A permanent-magnet (servo) motor that is turned by its load **generates** voltage at the drive's output terminals even with the drive off.
- **Disconnect the drive** before insulation-testing (meggering) the motor or its cable: 500 or 1000 V on the output terminals can destroy the drive.
- STO (safe torque off) stops torque; it does **not** isolate.
cards.more:
The bus of even a small drive holds hundreds of joules at 565 V: easily enough to kill. Bleed resistors discharge it over minutes, and if one has failed it may take much longer, so the measurement is the proof, not the clock.

STO removes the drive's ability to make torque (it blocks the gate signals), which is a safety function for stopping the machine. The motor terminals and the bus are still live.

For insulation tests, lift the motor cable at the drive end (or the motor end, and test the cable and motor separately). Test phase to phase and each phase to earth, at the voltage your test procedure gives.

cards.q: You suspect a motor's insulation after an earth fault trip. Before insulation testing the motor cable, what must you do?
options: Disconnect the cable from the drive
Switch the drive to its STO state
Set the drive's output frequency to zero
Remove the drive's brake resistor
cards.why: An insulation tester puts 500 or 1000 V DC on the conductors; at the drive's output terminals it can destroy the output transistors. Disconnect the cable from the drive (after isolating and checking the bus is discharged). STO and zero frequency leave it connected.

cards.q: Before changing any of a drive's parameters, what should you do first?
options: Save a copy of the parameters
Reset the drive to its factory settings
Run the identification run again
Nothing: the keypad can undo it
cards.why: A backup is the one sure way back. A factory reset throws away the motor data and the setup; most keypads cannot undo a change.

cards.q: Entering motor data for a motor wired in delta on a 400 V drive. The plate reads: 400 V Δ / 690 V Y, 14.6 / 8.4 A, 7.5 kW, 1455 rpm, cos φ 0.84. One entry is wrong. Which?
cards.fix: Rated current: 14.6 A (the delta figure, for 400 V)
cards.why: Wired delta on 400 V, the motor draws the 400 V current, 14.6 A. 8.4 A belongs to 690 V in star. With 8.4 A entered, the drive's motor protection trips at about half load. Check: $\frac{7500}{\sqrt{3} \times 400 \times 0.84 \times 0.89} \approx 14.5$ A.

cards.q: A drive is run over a fieldbus. Its 'communication loss' reaction is set to 'keep running at the last speed'. Why might that be a problem?
options: The PLC could no longer stop it over the bus
The drive will trip on overcurrent at once
The motor will reverse direction
Nothing: it is the safest setting
cards.why: With the bus down, the PLC's stop command never arrives, so the machine carries on unattended. Most machines should stop (ramp down or coast) on comms loss; keep-running suits only a few, such as some fans. (Emergency stops never rely on the fieldbus in any case.)

cards.q: A conveyor motor has been slowed to 15 Hz for a new product and now trips on motor overtemperature. The load is the same. Why?
options: Its shaft fan moves far less air at low speed
Lower frequency raises the supply voltage
The motor makes less torque, so it draws less current
The thermistor reads high at low frequency
cards.why: A standard motor is cooled by a fan on its own shaft; at 15 Hz it turns at 30% speed and moves much less air, while the torque, and so the current and heat, stay the same. Fit a separately powered fan, or a bigger motor.

cards.q: A drive trips on overcurrent only while starting a heavy flywheel. The fault log shows the trip at 8 Hz, rising. What is the likely cause?
options: The acceleration ramp is too short
The deceleration ramp is too short
The supply voltage is too high
The encoder is dirty
cards.why: Speeding up a big inertia quickly needs a lot of torque, so a lot of current. The log says it was accelerating. Lengthen the ramp (or raise the current limit within the drive's and motor's ratings).

cards.intro: A conveyor on a drive, run by a PLC. It has been reported as "not right". Run it as the operator would: Start, Stop, watch a box go through, lift it off. Read the drive, the lamps and the PLC's tags.

ask.why: Fault-finding is the same every time: see the symptom for yourself, then split the system in half. Here: does the PLC ask for Run? Does the drive follow? Does the belt follow the drive?

cards.intro: Someone has set this drive up. Every time it starts, it trips almost at once.

ask.q: Find out what it trips on. Then change one parameter so that it starts cleanly, and run the belt at full speed.
fails: The drive has tripped ({vfd.fault}). Reset it, change something, and start it again.
It is not running: press Start.
Nearly: it is still ramping up. Wait for it, then check.
ask.hint: Start it and read the fault code. OC means the current went over the drive's limit: what makes a motor draw a lot of current while it speeds up?
ask.why: OC on starting means the ramp asks for more torque than the motor can give without a huge current: here a heavy load and a 0.05 s ramp. Lengthen the acceleration time (2 s is plenty), or turn stall prevention (current limit) back on so the drive holds the ramp while the current is high. Either cures it; the longer ramp is kinder to the mechanics.

cards.q: A drive trips on DC overvoltage while running steadily at full speed, with no deceleration. What is the most likely cause?
options: A high or swelling mains supply
The deceleration ramp is too short
The acceleration ramp is too short
A dirty heatsink
cards.why: With no slowing down, the energy is not coming from the motor. The bus follows the mains: a high or swelling supply (or one with spikes from capacitor switching) can push it to the trip level. Measure the supply.

cards.q: A drive's current limit is set to {pc}% of a motor rated {ia} A. What is the limit in amps?
cards.why: Percentages in drive parameters are usually of the motor's rated current, as entered in the motor data. Another reason to enter it right.
cards.hint: Per cent of the rated current.

cards.q: Match each stop mode with what it does.
pairs: Slows along the deceleration ramp to zero
Cuts the output; the load runs down by itself
Ramps or cuts, then holds with DC injection
cards.why: Ramp stops are controlled but can regenerate; coast stops never regenerate but take as long as the load likes.

cards.q: Why keep a backup of every drive's parameters?
options: A replacement can be made to run the same, fast
Drives forget their settings every year
It makes the drive run more efficiently
The motor needs it to start
cards.why: When a drive fails, loading the backup into the new one gets the machine running in minutes, with the same motor data, ramps and I/O.

cards.q: {p} kW, 400 V, cos φ 0.85, 90% efficient. Full-load current?
cards.why: Power over √3 × V × power factor × efficiency.

cards.q: Match each trip with what to check first.
pairs: The acceleration ramp and the load
The deceleration ramp and the brake resistor
Motor and cable insulation, drive disconnected
The supply: dips and missing phases

cards.q: A drive has been isolated for a minute. Is it safe to touch its DC bus terminals?
options: No: wait the label's time, then measure
Yes: isolating it discharges the bus
Yes, if the keypad display is off
Yes, if STO is active
cards.why: The capacitors hold a lethal charge for minutes after isolation. A blank display does not mean a discharged bus. Wait, then prove it with a meter.
